There was once a grasshopper and a centipede. Summer was upon them, and the bounty of the land was plentiful. The centipede, taking full advantage of his opportunity, nimbly worked to secure a home for himself and his family, knowing it would never get any easier to prepare for the future than during the time of plenty. He ate, played, and engaged in the joys of life when he could, but remained dedicated to creating long-term prosperity and security, for he knew the winter would surely come.

Meanwhile, the grasshopper, awed by the bounty and beauty around him, danced and sang his days away, obeying his every desire whenever possible. "Why should I subject myself to the unpleasant-ness of labor," he said to himself, "when the world is such an happy and harmonious place? I can find a morsel of food here, an oasis of water there. It is simply there, free for the taking. Nature will provide for me."

One day, the grasshopper came upon the home of the centipedes and, seeing their magnificent infrastructure and acquired wealth, thought to himself; "This place is even more lovely than the wild! I must become part of their society, part of their home, so as to reap the benefits of their labor. Then I can sing and dance, obeying my every heart's desire, all through the year!"

The centipede was welcoming of the grasshopper, thinking he would help contribute in a way he himself could not. "It is a good thing," he reasoned, "to have someone nearby who is so joyous and full of wonder at life's beauty. I cannot partake in frivolity as much as he does, for I must toil and provide for my family, but having him around helps remind me of the joys of life." The summer went on, and all was well - the centipede continued to Make His Home Great, while enjoying the artistic fruits of the grasshopper.

But when autumn came, as must happen, the grasshopper grew nervous. His contributions became less and less valuable, as food and water were more scarce and staying warm became more and more of a challenge. The grasshopper had grown accustomed to living a life of privilege, and ate, danced and sang just as much as he had during the summer. Fearing that those whose fruits had enabled him to live in moral luxury would soon grow tired of his unwillingness to do the labor of survival, an idea came to the grasshopper. "I will tell them what they must do, what they must think, who they must feed," he thought, "so that they cannot punish me for singing and dancing all day when there is work to be done. I will appeal to their sense of fairness, for do I not also deserve to live?"

The centipede, upon hearing the grasshopper's insistence that Grasshopper Lives Matter, acquiesced, though there was something disquieting about this notion that he just could not put his Hollow Fangs on. He was unable to take the time to sort through it, however, and continued on working to provide for his family. "I suppose," he mused, "that the grasshopper does deserve to eat and drink in relative warmth and safety. Who am I to deny him these things? Besides, the younger centipedes seem to love him, and they need the comforts of his song and dance, for they are not yet as hardy or as nimble as I. Though I do wish he would eat a little bit less, dance a little bit less, and help out with the business of ensuring prosperity, if only on occasion. Surely he is capable of acquiring food and water, or helping build up our home? Surely he has some interest, now that this is his home as well, in doing his part to help us all survive the coming winter?"

The days grew shorter and colder, and still the grasshopper insisted on maintaining his lifestyle. By now, the centipede was actively grumbling, and began to eye the grasshopper with suspicion and resentment. "I love music and joy as much as the next bug, but I cannot put such frivolities ahead of mine and my family's survival." The grasshopper, sensing his imminent expulsion and resulting demise, became zealous in insisting that others provide for him. It was his livelihood, after all. He was no longer so frivolous and joyful, and his songs became low-energy and filled with hate. The grasshopper had given up his old role as entertainer, instead spending most of his days lecturing the centipedes on how unfair it was that they had more than he. "You didn't build that," he told the centipedes. "If you're a centipede, you don't know what it's like to be poor."

"That does it," said the centipede. "I don't wish to deprive this grasshopper fellow of anything that is rightly his, but what has he done beyond living off of our labors? None of the food, none of the water, and none of this home that protects us was built by him in any way. We cannot eat songs, and dancing will not keep the birds and lizards away. We would not expect him to be as nimble as us, since he does nothing but dance and sing and, of late, lecture us on how evil we are, but surely he could pitch in something."

The centipede made his feelings known to the grasshopper and, giving him one final chance said, "You will either contribute or you will leave, by force if necessary. We provide the things which keep you in your lackadaisical lifestyle, and in return you lecture us that it is not enough. We have more than you because we work for it - we cannot eat songs, and dancing will not keep the birds and lizards away. Winter is coming, and your frivolity has no place here now." The grasshopper was livid! Having mostly given up dancing and singing, he saw his very real plight and focused all of his efforts on lecturing. When this had little effect, he began to attack the centipedes, insisting with more zeal and fervor than ever that he was owed the fruits of their labor.

By now, of course, winter was in full swing, and the centipede and his family had had enough. They cornered the grasshopper and forcibly ejected him from their home. They made the entrances too small for the grasshopper to come back in, for they could navigate through brush while the grasshopper was inflexible. They posted centipede guards to make sure he could not sneak back in or damage their home. The centipedes, though they did not wish for the grasshopper to die, were relieved to no longer be supporting someone who would not give anything in return, and they lived comfortably through the winter.

The grasshopper, having nothing and no knowledge of how to survive, grew tired and cold very quickly. "Curse those centipedes!" yelled the grasshopper, feeling death's grip approach. "I will get back in and force them to see why my life is more imp-" The grasshopper was eaten by a bird. THE END
